html:
The Colombian conflict is the long armed conflict in Colombia between the state, left-wing guerrillas, right-wing paramilitaries and drug-trafficking groups. It began in the mid-1960s and has not fully ended. It has killed several hundred thousand people and driven millions from their homes.

Its roots lie in La Violencia, the war between Liberals and Conservatives from 1948 to 1958, and in unequal land. In 1964 armed peasants founded the FARC, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and the ELN, the National Liberation Army, followed. From the 1980s the coca and cocaine trade paid for all sides. Landowners and drug lords built paramilitary armies, which joined into one force in 1997 and carried out many massacres. From 2000 the United States paid for a large build-up of the army.

Indigenous and Afro-Colombian peoples were caught in the middle. The Emberá Katío, Nukak, Awá and Barí lost land and leaders, and many families fled to the cities.

The paramilitaries disarmed between 2003 and 2006. In 2016 the FARC signed a peace agreement with the government and became a political party. The ELN and breakaway groups fight on.
